# Clinical Trials in Practice: From Foundations to AI Agents

Alexandra Sokolova and Vadim Sokolov. Independently published, 2026. Edition 1, version 1.0.0. DOI: [10.5281/zenodo.23330460](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23330460).

Clinical trials are how medicine finds out what works, and they are slow, expensive, and tightly regulated. A well run trial can show that a treatment extends life or eases suffering. A poorly designed one can hide a real benefit, miss a serious harm, or spend years and produce nothing usable.

This book treats clinical trials as science and as regulated operations, and it gives Phase III the most room, because that is where approval is won or lost. It starts with how clinical research took its present shape, the drug development lifecycle, the regulatory frame, and the ethics of research with human subjects. It then follows a compound through the economics of development and Phases I to IV. The core of the book is the confirmatory trial: statistical foundations, adaptive and Bayesian designs, study design, real world evidence, randomization, endpoints, site selection, recruitment, logistics, data management, monitoring, safety reporting, essential documents, and the systems underneath. The closing chapters cover trial closeout, the clinical study report, and regulatory submission.

Methodology, operations, and technology are treated together. Where the book turns to automation and AI agents, one test applies: the tool must stand up in an inspection, with validation, governance, and a named person accountable for each decision.

It is written for medical directors, study managers, investigators and site staff, and for students and managers deciding whether AI has a place in regulated research.

## Building

The book is a Quarto project (Quarto 1.8 or later).

The online edition builds from this repository with Quarto alone. The figures drawn in R (ggplot2, tidyr and patchwork) are frozen in `_freeze/`, so R is not needed, and the workflow in `.github/workflows/pages.yml` runs the same two commands on every push and publishes `_book/`:

```bash
printf 'execute:\n  freeze: true\n' > _quarto-htmlfreeze.yml
quarto render --to html --profile htmlfreeze -M book-has-isbn:false
```

The PDF is typeset with XeLaTeX and the `krantz` class (`documentclass: krantz` in `_quarto.yml`). The class file `krantz.cls` is a typesetter file and is not part of this repository, so the PDF cannot be rebuilt from a clone until you supply that file in the project folder. The PDF of each release (`pdf/clinical_trials_in_practice.pdf`) is the built book. With the class file in place, the 7 x 10 in layout of the `kdp` profile builds with:

```bash
QUARTO_PROFILE=kdp quarto render --to pdf
```

This writes `_book-kdp/Clinical-Trials-in-Practice.pdf`. Without the profile, the render uses the default format in `_quarto.yml` (a US Letter page with trim marks) and writes to `_book/`.

What the PDF build needs:

- A TeX Live or TinyTeX installation with XeLaTeX, and `krantz.cls`.
- A headless Chromium for the Mermaid diagrams: `quarto install chromium`, or set `QUARTO_CHROMIUM` to a Chrome headless shell.
- R is not needed with the `kdp` profile: Quarto reuses the frozen results in `_freeze/` while the source of their chapter is unchanged. After editing `06-economics.qmd`, `11-statistical-methods.qmd`, `16-site-selection.qmd`, `17-recruitment.qmd` or `18-logistics.qmd`, refresh the frozen results of both formats with R and those three packages installed: render to PDF once with the `kdp` profile, and to HTML once with `execute: freeze: auto` in a profile file of your own. Without the profile, every render runs the R code.
